Applied Bayesian Inference · Chapter 3

Chapter 3
Bayesian linear models

Lectures 5–6 · the Gaussian model, the regression line, and what a coefficient means once the graph is drawn

More published science rests on the linear model than on any other statistical tool. It is the first model taught and the last one abandoned, and it is almost always the right place to begin. Its form is simple: the average of an outcome is a straight-line function of some predictors, and the outcomes scatter around that average with a bell-shaped spread. Every model in the rest of these notes, from logistic regression to neural networks, is a linear model with something changed.

The linear model's simplicity is also its trap. Fitting a line is easy; knowing what the fitted numbers mean is not. A regression of weight on height returns a slope of about 0.9 kg per centimetre. Is that how much heavier you would become if you grew a centimetre? How much heavier a taller person is, on average, among people like those in the sample? How much of the difference between men and women it explains? These are different questions, and the same coefficient answers at most one of them. Which one depends on the causal graph, not on the regression output. This chapter teaches the linear model and its Bayesian estimation, but its central lesson is the one in the cartoon: a coefficient is an answer, and the graph tells you which question it answers.

  • Lecture 5 builds the model. We will see why bell curves turn up everywhere, estimate the average height of American women from a national health survey (finding a trap in the data on the way), fit a line relating weight to height, separate the two kinds of uncertainty every prediction carries, and use a residual check to discover that the 19th-century formula for the body mass index is not quite right.
  • Lecture 6 asks what the coefficients mean. We will add a categorical predictor, separate a total effect from a direct one, watch a striking association between college majors and earnings shrink by half when we account for field of study, learn which "control variables" help and which do harm, and bend the line into a curve to measure when children grow fastest.

Think About It: Before You Start

Men in the United States are, on average, about 12 kg heavier than women. Men are also about 14 cm taller. Suppose you fit a regression of weight on sex and height. What do you expect the coefficient on sex to be, and what question would that number answer? Write down your guess; Section 3.7 gives the answer from data on 4,600 adults.
